Yliana: Probably a modern variant of Iliana or Juliana, blending Greek and Latin elements. Origin uncertain; Juliana derives from Latin Julius.
Gill: English short form of Gillian (Latin Juliana) or Gilbert, Germanic 'pledge, bright'. In Belgium also used as a short form of Gilles.
Sanaa: Arabic, meaning 'brilliance' or 'radiance'. Also the name of the capital of Yemen.
Loeka: Probably a Dutch or Flemish diminutive of Louise or Lucas, related to Latin Lucia 'light'. Origin uncertain.
Mazarine: French, from the surname Mazarin, borne by Cardinal Mazarin. Of Italian origin; the Mazarine Library in Paris carries it.
Mitch: English short form of Mitchell, itself a Middle English form of Michael, from Hebrew 'who is like God?'.
Loana: Modern coined name, possibly from Lo(ui)se with Ana, or from Hawaiian-style 'loa'. Origin uncertain.
Mattice: Probably a Dutch variant of Matthijs or Matthias, from Hebrew 'gift of God'. Origin uncertain.
Selen: Turkish, from Greek Selene, meaning 'moon'. In Turkish also used for 'torrent, flood'.
Cassie: English short form of Cassandra or Katherine. Cassandra is Greek, the Trojan prophetess.
Jody: English, a pet form of Joseph or Judith, used for both sexes. Hebrew, 'God will add' or 'praised'.
Clotilde: French form of Germanic Chlothilde, from hlod 'famous' and hild 'battle'. Borne by the wife of King Clovis.
Célina: French form of Celina, a feminine of Célin, from Latin Caelinus, from caelum 'sky, heaven'. Sometimes a short form of Marcelina.
Sarina: Variant of Sarah, Hebrew for 'princess'. Also used in Italy and the Netherlands.
Mathisse: Probably a Flemish variant of Mathis or Matthias, from Hebrew 'gift of God'. Origin uncertain.
Mélinda: French form of Melinda, a modern English blend probably of Greek meli 'honey' and the ending -inda.
Catharina: Latinised form of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine, of uncertain origin and long linked to katharos 'pure'.
Melinda: Modern English name, probably combining Greek meli 'honey' with the ending -inda. Possibly influenced by Linda.
Meriam: Arabic and Dutch form of Miriam, from Hebrew Miryam, meaning uncertain; often 'beloved' or 'bitter'.
Michele: Italian form of Michael (male), from Hebrew 'who is like God?'. As a girl's name it is the French and English feminine.
Nawel: Arabic (Nawal), meaning 'gift' or 'present'. Common among North African families.
Olaf: Scandinavian, from Old Norse Anleifr, 'ancestor's heirloom'. Borne by several Norwegian kings and Saint Olaf.
Syrine: Probably a variant of Sirine or Shirin, Persian-Arabic 'sweet'. Also linked to the French Syrinx 'reed pipe'. Origin uncertain.
Dave: English short form of David, Hebrew for 'beloved'.
Sita: Sanskrit, meaning 'furrow'. The heroine of the Ramayana, wife of Rama.
Tycho: Latinised Danish, from Greek Tykhon, from tyche 'luck, fortune'. Famous from astronomer Tycho Brahe.
Diete: Dutch, a short form of Dieuwertje or Diederike, Germanic theud 'people' and rik 'ruler'.
Marilyn: English, a combination of Mary and Lynn. Hebrew Miriam, meaning uncertain, is the root of Mary.
Lorys: Probably a variant of Lorris or Loris, from Italian Lorenzo or Latin Laurentius, 'from Laurentum'. Origin uncertain.
Matts: Scandinavian and Dutch short form of Matthias, from Hebrew 'gift of God'.
Tyson: English surname from Old French tison 'firebrand', or 'son of Dye'. Used as a given name after the boxer Mike Tyson.
Nolann: Modern Breton-style spelling of Nolan, from Irish Ó Nualláin, perhaps 'little champion'. Origin uncertain.
Arvid: Scandinavian, from Old Norse arn 'eagle' and viðr 'tree', or 'eagle of the people'.
Josué: French and Spanish form of Joshua, Hebrew Yehoshua, 'God is salvation'.
Loïse: French variant of Louise, feminine of Louis, from Germanic hlod 'famous' and wig 'battle'.
Mattiz: Modern variant of Matthias, from Hebrew 'gift of God'. Creative spelling.
Séréna: French form of Serena, from Latin serenus 'calm, clear, serene'.
Joé: French form of Joe, a short form of Joseph, Hebrew 'God will add'.
Sylvia: Latin, from silva 'forest'. Rhea Silvia was the mother of Romulus and Remus.
Diede: Dutch, short form of Diederike or Diederik, from Germanic theud 'people' and rik 'ruler'.
Leeloo: Modern coined name popularised by the film The Fifth Element. Possibly a variant of Lilou. Origin uncertain.
Leticia: Spanish and Portuguese form of Latin Laetitia, meaning 'joy, gladness'.
Melda: Probably a short form of Melinda or Mathilda. Also Turkish Melda, of uncertain origin. Origin uncertain.
Sen: Japanese 'thousand' or 'spring', and Dutch use as a short form of names like Senna. Origin varies; uncertain.
Davide: Italian form of David, Hebrew for 'beloved'.
Curtis: English, from Old French curteis 'courteous, refined'. Originally a surname.
Douae: Arabic Doaa or Dua, meaning 'prayer, supplication'. Spelling follows French transcription.
Erwin: Germanic, from hari 'army' and wini 'friend'. Also used in Dutch regions.
Eulalie: French form of Greek Eulalia, from eu 'well' and lalein 'to speak', so 'well-spoken'.
Shani: Hebrew, meaning 'scarlet' or 'crimson'. In Swahili it means 'marvellous'.
Zjef: Flemish short form of Jozef, from Hebrew Yosef, 'God will add'.
Constant: French and Dutch, from Latin constans, meaning 'steadfast, constant'.
Svea: Scandinavian, referring to the Svear (Swedes), the ancient Swedish people. Also a poetic personification of Sweden.
Denise: French feminine of Denis, from Greek Dionysios, 'follower of Dionysus', god of wine.
Lenke: Probably a Dutch or Frisian diminutive of Helena or Magdalena. Hungarian Lenke also exists. Origin uncertain.
Rien: Dutch short form of Marinus or Corrie-type names, also feminine of Katrien. Marinus is Latin, 'of the sea'.
Latifa: Arabic, meaning 'gentle, kind, delicate'. Feminine of Latif.
Soukayna: Arabic Sukayna, a diminutive of sakina meaning 'tranquillity, peace'. Borne by a granddaughter of Muhammad.
Jorik: Dutch and Russian form of George, from Greek georgos 'farmer'.
Iljo: Probably a modern variant of Elio or Iljo, linked to Greek helios 'sun' or Ilya (Elijah). Origin uncertain.
Katarina: Scandinavian and Slavic form of Katherine, from Greek Aikaterine, of uncertain origin.
Ioannis: Greek form of John, from Hebrew Yohanan, 'God is gracious'.
Iona: Scottish, from the island Iona, meaning perhaps 'yew place' in Gaelic. Also Greek ion 'violet'.
Lamya: Arabic, meaning 'radiant' or 'dark-lipped', a classical beauty ideal.
Pamela: English, invented by Sir Philip Sidney in the 16th century, probably from Greek pan 'all' and meli 'honey'.
Ditte: Danish and Dutch short form of Dorothea or Birgitte. Dorothea is Greek, 'gift of God'.
Lothar: Germanic, from hlod 'famous' and hari 'army'. Borne by Frankish kings.
Mellina: Probably a variant of Melina or Melinda, from Greek meli 'honey'. Origin uncertain.
Frank: Germanic, meaning 'free man' or 'Frank' (member of the Franks). Also a short form of Francis.
Han: Dutch short form of Johan or Johannes, Hebrew 'God is gracious'. Also a Chinese surname and given name.
Kelvin: Scottish, from the River Kelvin, of uncertain meaning. Made famous by Lord Kelvin.
Maximiliaan: Dutch form of Maximilian, from Latin Maximilianus, derived from Maximus 'greatest'.
Haytam: Arabic, from Haytham, meaning 'young eagle' or 'young falcon'.
Laureline: French, a compound of Laure and the ending -line. Laure is from Latin laurus 'laurel'.
Helene: Greek, probably meaning 'torch' or 'bright one'. Helen of Troy is the best-known bearer.
Abdelkader: Arabic Abd al-Qadir, 'servant of the Capable', one of the names of God.
Anika: Scandinavian and German diminutive of Anna, from Hebrew Hannah, 'grace'. Also Sanskrit for 'army'.
Heike: Low German and Frisian diminutive of Heinrike or Hendrika, from Germanic heim 'home' and rik 'ruler'.
Joakim: Scandinavian form of Joachim, Hebrew 'God will establish'.
Karima: Arabic, meaning 'generous' or 'noble', feminine of Karim.
Matthys: Dutch form of Matthias, from Hebrew 'gift of God'.
Merle: German and French, from Latin merula 'blackbird'.
Chana: Hebrew form of Hannah, meaning 'grace' or 'favour'. Also Thai 'victory'.
Emmelien: Dutch variant of Emmeline or Emelie, from Germanic amal 'work, labour'. Emilia is Latin 'rival'.
Karolina: Latinised feminine of Charles, from Germanic karl 'free man'. Common in Poland and Scandinavia.
Kyandro: Modern coined name, possibly from Alexandro or Cassandro. Origin uncertain.
Thao: Vietnamese, meaning 'respectful of parents' or 'herb, grass'. Used for both sexes.
Valérian: French, from Latin Valerianus, a derivative of Valerius, from valere 'to be strong'.
Kara: Several origins: Greek 'pure' or 'dear', Italian cara 'beloved', or a Danish short form of Katherine. Uncertain.
Süleyman: Turkish form of Solomon, from Hebrew Shlomo, 'peaceful'.
Sema: Turkish, from Arabic sama, meaning 'sky, heaven'.
Shanaya: Probably an Indian name, perhaps 'first ray of sun' or from Sanskrit. Origin uncertain.
Rayhan: Arabic Rayhan, meaning 'sweet basil' or 'fragrance'. Mentioned in the Quran.
Alizé: French, from alizé 'trade wind', a gentle steady wind of the tropics.
Hiranur: Turkish, probably Hira, the cave of Muhammad's first revelation, plus nur 'light'.
Liesel: German diminutive of Elisabeth, from Hebrew 'my God is an oath'.
Matys: Variant of Mathys or Matthias, from Hebrew 'gift of God'. Popular in France.
Tygo: Dutch modern form, probably from Tycho (Greek tyche 'luck') or Thijs. Origin uncertain.
Lentl: Probably a Flemish variant of Lente, Dutch for 'spring'. Origin uncertain.
Cansu: Turkish, from can 'life, soul' and su 'water', so 'water of life'.
Domenico: Italian form of Dominic, from Latin dominicus 'of the Lord'.
Liselot: Dutch compound of Lies (Elisabeth) and Lot (Charlotte). Hebrew and Germanic elements.
Mackenzie: Scottish, from Gaelic Mac Coinnich, 'son of Coinneach', meaning 'handsome, comely'. Used for girls in Belgium.
Silvio: Italian form of Silvius, from Latin silva 'forest'.
Ella-Louise: English double name: Ella, from Germanic ali 'other' or Eleanor, and Louise, feminine of Louis.
Ileana: Romanian and Spanish form of Helena, probably Greek 'torch'.
Pierrot: French diminutive of Pierre, from Greek petros 'rock'. Also the sad clown of French theatre.
Iness: Variant of Inès or Agnes, Greek hagnos 'pure'.
Romayssa: Arabic Rumaysa, a Companion's name, probably from a word for a small sweet-smelling plant. Origin uncertain.
Doris: Greek, 'woman of Doris' or 'gift', from doron. In myth, a sea nymph.
Guy: French, from Germanic Wido, possibly 'wood' or 'wide'. Also English from Hebrew-based Guido.
Nazli: Turkish, meaning 'coy, delicate, graceful', from Persian naz.
Berkan: Turkish, from berk 'solid, firm' and the ending -an. Modern Turkish name.
Troy: English, from the Irish surname Ó Troightigh 'foot soldier', or after the city of Troy. Also French Troyes.
Mart: Dutch short form of Maarten or Martinus, from Latin Mars. Also Estonian short form.
Sania: Arabic Saniyya, meaning 'brilliant, lofty'. Also Slavic 'Sanja' as short form of Aleksandra.
Ketsia: Variant of Keziah, Hebrew for 'cassia', a spice tree. Biblical daughter of Job.
Kyran: Variant of Kieran, from Irish Ciarán, 'little dark one'.
Maroua: Arabic Marwa, a hill near Mecca. Possibly meaning 'flint' or 'fragrant plant'.
Mikaël: French form of Michael, from Hebrew 'who is like God?'.
Thorsten: Scandinavian, from Old Norse Thor 'thunder' and steinn 'stone'.
Eglantine: French, from the word for the wild rose or sweetbriar, from Latin aculeus 'prickly'.
Hasna: Arabic, meaning 'beautiful, good'. Feminine of Hasan.
Patryk: Polish form of Patrick, from Latin patricius 'nobleman'.
Ryad: Arabic Riyad, meaning 'gardens', plural of rawda.
Yolan: Possibly a variant of Yolande or Jolan, French and Hungarian, perhaps from Greek 'violet flower'. Origin uncertain.
Aurian: Probably a variant of Adrian or Aurélien, from Latin aureus 'golden'. Origin uncertain.
Erwann: Breton form of Erwan or Yves, perhaps from Celtic 'yew'. Origin uncertain.
Kessy: Probably a variant of Kessie or a diminutive of Kesia, from Hebrew 'cassia'. Origin uncertain.
Thorgan: Probably a modern blend of Thor with Morgan, or Scandinavian torgeir. Origin uncertain.
Wail: Arabic Wa'il, meaning 'one who seeks refuge'.
Zias: Probably a modern short form of Zacharias, Hebrew 'God remembers'. Origin uncertain.
Elynn: Modern variant of Eileen or Elin, from Helen 'torch'. Origin uncertain.
Sonny: English diminutive meaning 'little son', used as an affectionate nickname.
Bayram: Turkish, meaning 'festival, holiday', as in Eid.
Chaymae: Arabic Shaymaa, a Companion's name, meaning 'one with a beauty mark'. Spelling follows French transcription.
Louize: Dutch variant of Louise, feminine of Louis, from Germanic hlod 'famous' and wig 'battle'.
Sibe: Frisian, a short form of Sibo or Sibbe, from Germanic sibja 'kinship, peace'.
Sybe: Frisian variant of Sibe, from Germanic sibja 'kin' or 'peace'.
Anne-Marie: French compound of Anne (Hebrew 'grace') and Marie (Hebrew Miriam).
Anyssa: Probably a variant of Anissa, Arabic 'friendly companion', or of Alyssa. Origin uncertain.
Leena: Finnish and Estonian short form of Helena. Also Arabic 'tender, soft'.
Lilli: German diminutive of Elisabeth or Lilian, or from lily, Latin lilium.
Meyssa: Arabic Maysa, meaning 'walking proudly' or 'swaying'. Also Maisa.
Ceylan: Turkish, meaning 'gazelle'. Also the old name of Sri Lanka.
Naima: Arabic, meaning 'tranquil, comfortable'. Also a feminine of Naim.
Nuria: Spanish, from a Catalan Marian title Mare de Déu de Núria. Arabic nur 'light' likely related.
Teresa: Spanish and Portuguese, possibly from Greek therizein 'to harvest' or the island Thera. Origin uncertain.
Dawid: Polish and Afrikaans form of David, from Hebrew 'beloved'.
Anes: Arabic Anas, meaning 'friendliness, affection'. Anas ibn Malik was a Companion of Muhammad.
Kane: Irish and English, from Ó Catháin 'descendant of Cathán', 'battle'. Hawaiian kane means 'man'.
Stephan: German form of Stephen, from Greek stephanos 'crown, wreath'.
Yelina: Probably a Slavic or modern variant of Elena, from Greek 'torch'. Origin uncertain.
Dilay: Turkish, probably from dil 'heart, tongue' and ay 'moon'. Modern coinage.
Leelou: Modern French spelling of Lilou, a diminutive of Louise or Élisabeth. Possibly a coined name.
Lynne: English, from Welsh llyn 'lake', or a short form of Lynn. Also a short form of Carolyn.
Moncef: Arabic Munsif, meaning 'just, fair'. Common in Tunisia.
Nouhaila: Arabic Nuhayla or Nuhaila, probably 'quenching thirst'. Origin uncertain; common in North Africa.
Soundous: Arabic Sundus, meaning 'fine silk, brocade'. Mentioned in the Quran as paradise garments.
Dwayne: Irish, from Ó Dubhán, 'little dark one'. Popularised as a given name in America.
Filippo: Italian form of Philip, from Greek philippos, 'lover of horses'.
Josef: German and Czech form of Joseph, Hebrew 'God will add'.
Nahla: Arabic, meaning 'a drink of water' or 'sip'.
Scout: English word name, from Old French escoute 'listener'. Made famous by the heroine of To Kill a Mockingbird.
Célio: Portuguese and French, from Latin Caelius, from caelum 'heaven, sky'. Also Italian Celio, a Roman hill.
Eliane: French feminine of Elie or Elian, from Hebrew Eliyahu, 'my God is Yahweh'.
Mateusz: Polish form of Matthew, from Hebrew 'gift of God'.
Yano: Probably a modern coined name; possibly a Dutch variant of Jano or Gianno, from John. Also Japanese surname. Origin uncertain.
Andrès: French and Spanish form of Andrew, from Greek andreios 'manly'.
Timéa: Hungarian, created by writer Mór Jókai, possibly from Greek time 'honour'. Origin uncertain.
Romaïssa: Arabic Rumaysa, a Companion's name, probably from a word for a small sweet-smelling plant. Origin uncertain.
Byron: English, from an Old English place name meaning 'at the cattle sheds', made famous by Lord Byron.
Clement: English and Dutch, from Latin clemens, meaning 'merciful, gentle'.
Hümeyra: Turkish, from Arabic Humayra, 'little red one', a nickname of Aisha. Origin classical.
Inna: Slavic, probably from Latin Innocentia or from Inna 'strong water'. Origin uncertain.
Loren: Variant of Lauren or Lorenzo, ultimately from Latin Laurentius, 'from Laurentum'.
Massimiliano: Italian form of Maximilian, from Latin Maximus 'greatest'.
Almir: Bosnian and Portuguese, from Arabic Amir 'prince' with a prefix, or 'the prince'. Origin partly uncertain.
Atakan: Turkish, from ata 'ancestor, father' and kan 'blood', so 'of noble blood'.
Chahine: Arabic Shahin, meaning 'falcon' or 'hawk'. Common in Lebanon and Egypt.
Elmedina: Bosnian, from Arabic al-Madina, 'the city', as in Medina. Used as a girl's name among Balkan Muslims.
Elyn: Modern variant of Elin or Eileen, from Helen 'torch'. Origin uncertain.
